# Graham and Svolik (2020): democracy and partisanship {#sec-gs}

@graham2020democracy ask whether voters punish candidates who violate democratic principles when
party and policy favor those candidates. Respondents chose between two hypothetical state
legislative candidates in up to thirteen matchups. The candidates differed in party, economic and
social policy, governance practices, democratic violations, scandals, and personal traits. This
chapter reproduces the paper's results for this experiment from the saved fit.

```{r}
#| label: gs-setup
#| cache: false
library(sconjoint)
fits <- getOption("sconjoint.fits", "fits")
gs <- sc_load(file.path(fits, "gs_q3.rds"))
if (is.null(gs)) stop("This chapter needs the saved fit gs_q3.rds; see the installation chapter.")
# a short table of estimates
tab <- function(e, digits = 3) {
  out <- e[, c("name", "estimate", "plug_in", "se", "lower", "upper", "n")]
  out[2:6] <- lapply(out[2:6], round, digits)
  out
}
```

## The data and the fit

`sc_example_data("gs")` builds the paper's inputs from the bundled `gs2020` data: 1,605
respondents, 20,657 matchups, and 30 coded features. The candidate shown on the left comes first,
so `y = 1` means the left candidate was chosen. The network sees sixteen respondent characteristics
measured before the tasks. The data also carry the paper's five folds, the respondents held out for
early stopping in each fold, and the grouping variables.

```{r}
#| label: gs-data
x <- sc_example_data("gs")
x
head(x$groups)
```

The groups are party ID (`pid7`, from -3 strong Democrat to 3 strong Republican), party (`party`,
with leaners counted as partisans), self-described ideology among all respondents (`ideology`), and
`PL`, which is 1 for the 1,377 partisans and leaners. The co-partisan feature is always zero for
the 228 pure independents, so their co-partisan taste cannot be learned from their choices.
Quantities about party therefore use `w = "PL"`.

The paper fitted the model at one to four taste factors and chose three. The defaults of `sc_fit()`
and `sc_states()` are the paper's settings, so the code below reproduces the saved fit. It takes
several hours and is not run here.

```{r}
#| label: gs-fit
#| eval: false
fit_q <- lapply(1:4, function(q) sc_fit(x, q = q))   # five folds at each rank
sc_select_rank(fit_q)
gs <- sc_states(fit_q[[3]])                           # q = 3; M = 300 designs, 4 responses each
sc_save(gs, file.path(fits, "gs_q3.rds"))
```

`sc_select_rank()` gives the paper's rank table:

| Taste factors | Held-out log score | Gain over $q - 1$ | Paired $z$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | -7.797 | | |
| 2 | -7.772 | 0.0249 | 2.19 |
| 3 (selected) | -7.739 | 0.0329 | 2.99 |
| 4 | -7.742 | -0.0029 | -0.47 |

The log score is the average log probability of a held-out respondent's whole sequence of choices.
The rule moves to $q = 3$ and stops because the fourth factor does not improve the fit.

## Mean tastes

A mean taste is the average utility a respondent gains from one coded feature, on the logit scale
of the model. `sc_mean()` takes the feature name. The co-partisan mean averages over partisans and
leaners; the others average over all respondents.

```{r}
#| label: gs-means
fn <- gs$data$data$feature_names
mean_targets <- lapply(fn, function(f) sc_mean(f, f, w = if (f == "diff_respParty") "PL" else NULL))
means <- sc_estimate(gs, mean_targets)
tab(means[c(1:3, 10:18), ])
```

Among partisans and leaners, a co-partisan candidate gains 0.81 units of utility on average. Each
step toward the conservative end of economic policy costs 0.24. All seven undemocratic actions
(`u_`) carry negative means, from -0.53 for the two-seat gerrymander to -0.90 for prosecuting
journalists. The two scandals (`v_`) cost -0.94 (an affair) and -1.18 (underpaid taxes). The
conduct codes are measured against the generic reference position, a candidate who supports an
elected oversight board. The `plug_in` column is the cross-fitted fitted value before the score
correction (@sec-inference).

## Preference shares

A mean can hide how many respondents are on each side. `sc_share()` estimates the share of
respondents whose taste for the contrast is positive. It averages over the fitted normal law of
each respondent's tastes.

```{r}
#| label: gs-shares
shares <- sc_estimate(gs, list(
  sc_share("co-partisan", "diff_respParty", w = "PL"),
  sc_share("economic policy, per point", "diff_p1_num"),
  sc_share("close polling stations", "diff_dem_code_u_limitVote"),
  sc_share("prosecute journalists", "diff_dem_code_u_journalists")))
tab(shares, 4)
```

An estimated 82.5% of partisans and leaners prefer a co-partisan, with a 95% interval from 79.7% to
84.9%. The share favoring a violation is close to zero, and then it is hard to pin down. For closing
polling stations the estimate is 7.3%, with a wide interval. For prosecuting journalists the
estimate is 0.2% and the interval runs from 0 to 1. When nearly everyone opposes an action, the
share depends on the spread of its taste across respondents. Each respondent saw each violation only
once, so that spread is measured imprecisely.

## Fitted distributions

`sc_fitted_law()` returns the fitted law of a taste: for each held-out respondent, a normal
distribution with that respondent's fitted mean and the spread implied by the taste factors. The
population law is the mixture of these normals.

```{r}
#| label: gs-laws
law_cp <- sc_fitted_law(gs, "diff_respParty", w = "PL")
law_j <- sc_fitted_law(gs, "diff_dem_code_u_journalists")
attr(law_cp, "summary")
head(law_cp)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-laws
#| fig-cap: "Fitted taste distributions in the democracy experiment"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.4
mix_density <- function(law, grid) {
  sapply(grid, function(t) mean(dnorm(t, law$mean, law$sd)))
}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 2, 0.8), cex = 0.85)
grid <- seq(-2.5, 4.5, length.out = 301)
plot(grid, mix_density(law_cp, grid), type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "#004a8c",
     xlab = "Taste for a co-partisan (logit utility)", ylab = "Density",
     main = "Co-partisan, partisans and leaners", font.main = 1)
abline(v = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
grid <- seq(-3.5, 1.5, length.out = 301)
plot(grid, mix_density(law_j, grid), type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "#004a8c",
     xlab = "Taste for prosecuting journalists (logit utility)", ylab = "Density",
     main = "Prosecuting journalists, all respondents", font.main = 1)
abline(v = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
par(op)
```

The left panel shows a wide spread: most partisans and leaners favor a co-partisan, some strongly,
and a minority are below zero. The right panel is narrow and almost entirely below zero. So the share
favoring prosecution sits near zero, where it is hard to estimate. These curves are fitted values
before the score correction, so their means can differ from the corrected means above.

## What can offset a violation

The paper asks whether a party advantage can outweigh a violation. Consider a co-partisan who
prosecutes journalists against an otherwise identical non-co-partisan at the generic reference
position. A respondent prefers the co-partisan when the sum of the two tastes is positive. The
*compensation share* is the share for whom that holds. In `sc_share()` the contrast is the sum of
the two features.

```{r}
#| label: gs-comp
g <- gs$data$groups
comp <- lapply(c(lib = "lib", mod = "mod", con = "con"), function(ideo)
  sc_share(paste("journalists + co-partisan,", ideo),
           c("diff_dem_code_u_journalists", "diff_respParty"),
           w = as.numeric(g$ideology == ideo) * g$PL))
comp_est <- sc_estimate(gs, comp)
tab(comp_est)
```

An estimated 33.8% of liberal partisans and leaners and 59.6% of conservative ones prefer the
co-partisan who prosecutes journalists. The same party advantage outweighs the violation for many
respondents, even though the violation's mean penalty is large.

The ratio of the two means compares their average sizes. `sc_ratio()` returns $-\tau_j / \tau_p$,
the mean prosecution penalty in units of the mean partisan gain, with a delta-method standard error.

```{r}
#| label: gs-ratio
price <- sc_ratio("journalists penalty / co-partisan gain",
                  sc_mean("journalists, partisans", "diff_dem_code_u_journalists", w = "PL"),
                  sc_mean("co-partisan", "diff_respParty", w = "PL"))
tab(sc_estimate(gs, price))
```

The ratio is 1.14 (95% interval 0.91 to 1.37): on average, the two are of similar size.

## Candidate contests

A contest is a specified matchup. `sc_contest()` estimates the expected share choosing the first
candidate, with position effects set to zero and task shocks kept. The paper places a co-partisan
at each social-policy position (1 most liberal, 4 most conservative) against a non-co-partisan at
position 3, with all other attributes equal. The co-partisan either has a clean record or
prosecutes journalists. The contrast vector is the coded difference between the two candidates.

```{r}
#| label: gs-contests
e <- function(f) as.numeric(fn %in% f)
contests <- list()
for (ideo in c("lib", "con")) for (violation in c("clean", "journalists")) for (pos in 1:4) {
  d <- e("diff_respParty") + (pos - 3) * e("diff_p2_num")
  if (violation == "journalists") d <- d + e("diff_dem_code_u_journalists")
  contests[[length(contests) + 1]] <- sc_contest(paste(ideo, violation, pos, sep = "."), d,
                                                 w = as.numeric(g$ideology == ideo) * g$PL)
}
contest_est <- sc_estimate(gs, contests)
wide <- matrix(round(100 * contest_est$estimate, 1), ncol = 4, byrow = TRUE,
               dimnames = list(c("liberal, clean", "liberal, journalists",
                                 "conservative, clean", "conservative, journalists"),
                               paste("position", 1:4)))
wide
```

At position 2, the co-partisan who prosecutes journalists receives an estimated 49.8% of support
among liberal partisans and leaners and 52.1% among conservative ones. Without the violation the
same candidate receives 74.2% and 67.7%. Prosecuting journalists costs about 24 and 16 points of
expected support. These are expected vote shares: they include task shocks, so they differ from the
compensation shares above. The intervals are in `contest_est`.

## Effects on choices

An average marginal effect (AME) switches one attribute of a candidate and averages the change in
the probability that the candidate is chosen over the experiment's other attributes and opponents.
It is the model's counterpart of the AMCE. `sc_ame_switch()` names the raw design attribute, the
level switched to and the reference level. For party, the level is the respondent's own party (1 =
Democrat, 2 = Republican in the raw design) and the reference is the other party; the switch is
undefined for pure independents.

```{r}
#| label: gs-ames
ames <- sc_estimate(gs, list(
  sc_ame_switch("co-partisan", "party",
                level = function(k) c(D = 1L, R = 2L, I = NA_integer_)[[k]],
                ref = function(k) c(D = 2L, R = 1L, I = NA_integer_)[[k]],
                design = "gs", w = "PL"),
  sc_ame_switch("prosecute journalists", "dem", "diff_dem_code_u_journalists", "g_boardElect",
                design = "gs")))
tab(ames)
```

A co-partisan candidate gains 14.0 percentage points of support, and a candidate who prosecutes
journalists loses 16.2 points. The paper reports regression AMCEs of 14.1 and -16.1 points for the
same populations. The model reproduces the familiar choice effects and adds the preferences behind
them.

## Attribute importance

Importance asks how much each attribute moves a respondent's utility over a stated menu of its
levels, as a share of the total. The paper uses seven attributes: party, the two four-point policy
scales, all fifteen governance, violation and scandal codes as one attribute, sex, race and
profession. A policy scale is coded by one column, so its menu is `matrix(1:4)`. The shares sum to
one and come from one joint update. The package reports them without intervals, because in the
paper's simulations their intervals cover less often than stated.

```{r}
#| label: gs-importance
attrs <- list(party = "diff_respParty", econ = "diff_p1_num", social = "diff_p2_num",
              conduct = grep("^diff_dem_code_", fn, value = TRUE),
              sex = grep("^diff_sex_", fn, value = TRUE),
              race = grep("^diff_race_", fn, value = TRUE),
              profession = grep("^diff_pro_", fn, value = TRUE))
imp <- sc_estimate(gs, sc_importance(attrs, menus = list(econ = matrix(1:4), social = matrix(1:4)),
                                     w = "PL"))
imp[, c("name", "estimate", "plug_in", "n", "status")]
```

```{r}
#| label: gs-importance-summary
s <- setNames(imp$estimate, imp$name)
round(100 * c(policy = s[["econ"]] + s[["social"]], party = s[["party"]],
              conduct = s[["conduct"]], background = s[["sex"]] + s[["race"]] + s[["profession"]]), 1)
```

Among partisans and leaners, policy accounts for 46.5% of utility variation, party for 32.9%,
governance and conduct for 18.3%, and background traits for 2.3%. The joint update took about eight
minutes. The party-specific shares use the same call with `w = function(g) g$party == "Dem"` or
`"Rep"`, one joint update each.

## Decisiveness of a swap

Decisiveness asks how often exchanging two candidates' levels on one attribute would reverse the
choice, holding the other attributes and the task shock fixed. It averages over the matchups each
respondent actually saw. The computation takes about twenty minutes for this experiment, so the code
is shown but not run.

```{r}
#| label: gs-decisiveness
#| eval: false
conduct <- grep("^diff_dem_code_", fn)
action <- grep("^diff_dem_code_[uv]_", fn[conduct])
generic <- c(TRUE, grepl("^diff_dem_code_g_", fn[conduct]))   # reference row plus generic codes
sc_estimate(gs, list(
  sc_decisiveness(list(party = "diff_respParty"), pairs = list(party = c(2L, 1L)),
                  names = "party", w = "PL"),
  sc_decisiveness(list(conduct = fn[conduct]), pairs = list(conduct = cbind(1L + action, 1L)),
                  allowed = list(conduct = generic),
                  names = sub("^diff_dem_code_[uv]_", "", fn[conduct][action]))))
```

The paper reports that exchanging party reverses 36.1% of choices among partisans and leaners (95%
interval 33.8% to 38.4%). Exchanging a candidate who prosecutes journalists with one at the generic
reference position reverses 32.0% (27.3% to 37.1%), the largest among the seven violations.

## The paper's full target list

The function below writes every GS quantity in the paper's main results file with the public
functions: a mean and a share for each of the 30 features, the compensation shares for seven
violations in three ideology groups, 24 contests, the switch AMEs and the ratio. With the bounded
updates for its 51 shares, `sc_estimate(gs, gs_targets(gs))` takes about 40 minutes and reproduces
the paper's estimates, standard errors and intervals.

```{r}
#| label: gs-full
#| eval: false
gs_targets <- function(st) {
  fn <- st$data$data$feature_names; g <- st$data$groups
  e1 <- function(j) as.numeric(seq_along(fn) == j)
  tl <- list(); add <- function(t) tl[[length(tl) + 1L]] <<- t
  for (j in seq_along(fn)) {
    w <- if (j == 1L) "PL" else NULL
    add(sc_mean(paste0(fn[j], ".mean"), fn[j], w)); add(sc_share(paste0(fn[j], ".share"), fn[j], w))
  }
  actions <- grep("^diff_dem_code_u_", fn)
  for (ideo in c("lib", "mod", "con")) {
    wi <- as.numeric(g$ideology == ideo) * g$PL
    for (j in actions) add(sc_share(paste0("comp.", ideo, ".", fn[j]), c(fn[j], fn[1L]), wi))
    for (violation in c("clean", "journalists")) for (pos in 1:4) {
      v <- e1(1L) + (pos - 3) * e1(3L)
      if (violation == "journalists") v <- v + e1(match("diff_dem_code_u_journalists", fn))
      add(sc_contest(paste0("contest.", ideo, ".", violation, ".", pos), v, w = wi))
    }
  }
  jm <- sc_mean("journalists.partisan.mean", "diff_dem_code_u_journalists", "PL"); add(jm)
  for (j in c(1:3, actions, grep("^diff_dem_code_v_", fn))) {
    if (j == 1L) {
      add(sc_ame_switch(paste0(fn[j], ".ame"), "party", function(k) c(D = 1L, R = 2L, I = NA_integer_)[[k]],
                        function(k) c(D = 2L, R = 1L, I = NA_integer_)[[k]], design = "gs", w = "PL"))
    } else if (j <= 3L) {
      add(sc_ame_switch(paste0(fn[j], ".ame"), paste0("p", j - 1L), 4L, 1L, design = "gs", scale = 1 / 3))
    } else {
      add(sc_ame_switch(paste0(fn[j], ".ame"), "dem", fn[j], "g_boardElect", design = "gs"))
    }
  }
  add(sc_ratio("journalists.party.price", jm, sc_mean("diff_respParty.mean", "diff_respParty", "PL")))
  tl
}
```

The policy AMEs switch a candidate from position 1 to position 4 and divide by three, so they are
per point of the scale.
